title: Reading a hung process
summary: Take a dump, find the threads that wait on each other with clrstack and syncblk, and fix the call-out-under-lock that caused it.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: a hang
steps.body: A service that is alive but answers nothing, with CPU near zero: take evidence first, then restart.

toolkit.what: A full dump of the hung process. In Kubernetes, run it inside the pod (or a debug container sharing its process namespace).
An SOS prompt over the dump. The commands below run inside it.
Every Monitor (lock statement on an object) that is held: owner thread and how many wait. MonitorHeld = 1 for the owner + 2 per waiter.
toolkit.when: a hang with low CPU in code that uses lock

toolkit.what: The managed stack of every thread. `pstacks` (parallelstacks) merges identical stacks into a tree.
flags: grouped view, like Visual Studio's Parallel Stacks
toolkit.when: find what each blocked thread is waiting for, and where in your code

toolkit.what: Async state machines that are not finished, with what each awaits. Async deadlocks hold no thread, so only this shows them.
toolkit.when: requests hang but clrstack shows idle pool threads

steps.prompt: Match the symptom to the first command you run in `dotnet-dump analyze`.
pairs: Hang, low CPU, the code uses `lock`
Requests hang, but no thread is blocked anywhere

steps.title: The evidence
body: The orders service hung at 14:02. From the dump:
Index         SyncBlock MonitorHeld Recursion Owning Thread Info          SyncBlock Owner
Read it: two locks are held, each with **one waiter** (MonitorHeld 3 = owner + 2 for one waiter). Thread 12 is inside `Reserve`
(holding the stock lock) and waits in `PriceBook.Touch` for the price lock. Thread 17 is inside `Reprice` (holding the price lock)
and waits in `Inventory.Count` for the stock lock. A cycle.
Note: locks on the .NET 9 `System.Threading.Lock` type are not Monitors, so they do **not** appear in `syncblk`; find them by the
threads whose stacks stop inside `System.Threading.Lock` methods.

steps.prompt: What is the root cause in this code?
options: Each class calls into the other while holding its own lock, so the two locks are taken in opposite orders
steps.explain: Neither class looks wrong on its own. The deadlock exists only in how they call each other: a call out while holding a lock. Fix the design: do not hold your lock while calling the other class.

steps.title: The same bug, live
body: Here are the two classes from the dump. Run **Try every interleaving** and find the deadlock, then step through it: watch which
lock each thread holds (the bands under the lanes) when they get stuck.

code: public int Count(string sku) { lock (_stockLock) return _stock; }

steps.prompt: Put the response to the 14:02 hang in order.
lines: Take a dump of the hung process (`dotnet-dump collect`)
Restart the instance to restore service
`syncblk` and `clrstack` in the dump: two threads, two locks, a cycle
Fix the code so neither class calls the other while holding its lock
Add a test that forces the interleaving, and a lock-wait timeout alert

steps.title: Break the cycle
prompt: Fix **`Inventory`** and **`PriceBook`** (the classes from the dump) so they can never deadlock, **without** a lock shared by both
classes. Keep every member's name and behaviour: `Reserve` takes one item from stock and touches the price book; `Reprice` bumps
the version if fewer than 10 are in stock.
**Checked:** `Reserve` and `Reprice` run at the same time under every interleaving. No deadlock, and the stock ends at 4.
starter: public int Count(string sku) { lock (_stockLock) return _stock; }
solution: Prices.Touch(sku);          // call out after releasing our lock
public int Count(string sku) { lock (_stockLock) return _stock; }
var count = Stock.Count(sku);   // ask the other class first, holding nothing
hints: A deadlock needs a thread holding one lock while waiting for the other. Can each method finish with its own lock before calling the other class?
In `Reserve`, call `Prices.Touch(sku)` after the `lock` block. In `Reprice`, read `Stock.Count(sku)` into a local before taking `_priceLock`.
explain: Reading the count before taking the lock means the decision may use a slightly old value. Here that is fine (repricing is
best effort); when it is not, you need one lock over both pieces of state, or a single owner of the data (an actor, a channel
